reward and punishment are not symmetric

obvious to most people, but why exactly?

reward incentives exploring similar behaviors

punishment disincentives exploring similar behaviors, and incentives exploring ways to evade it

so punishment can't be used for nuanced behaviors

│       *   **Explanation of Negative Feedback in Control Systems**
│           *   In control systems, negative refers to "going in the opposite direction of the gap". But if it's too cold, say -3 degrees, you need a change of +3 degrees. So either way the feedback opposes the measurement, which means multiplying by a negative number.
│       *   **Positive Feedback**
│           *   Whereas positive feedback is unrestricted growth, such as a virus spreading where the more virus there is out there, the faster it spreads—a positive multiplier.
│

Anchored by Qiaochu Yuan's 2021 observation and crystallized through Malcolm Ocean's 2022 phrase 'punishment can't steer because awayness can't aim,' the discourse moves from abstract systems theory to practical applications in parenting, self-motivation, AI training, and somatic healing. The narrative is highly dialectical—participants refine the concept through edge cases (hyperplanes, constraints, rewards vs towardsness) while maintaining cohesion around the core insight. High utility for anyone working with motivation systems, though primarily theoretical rather than producing physical artifacts.

title: “Punishment can’t steer” became the internet’s mantra
summary:
The quotable core that lit everything up: Malcolm Ocean’s line “Punishment can’t steer because awayness can’t aim.” The claim is basically geometry-as-psychology—fear/punishment pushes you *somewhere*, but in a high‑dimensional “behavior space” it’s under-specified, so you get flailing, loophole-hunting, and jittering. Desire/“towardsness” can actually point at a target. This started back in 2021 when CountJ0ecool framed negative reinforcement as “large divergence away from a point” vs positive as a “uniform vector field,” echoing Qiaochu Yuan’s earlier observation that “avoid” has too many directions. Adele Dewey Lopez then made it concrete: rewards make you explore nearby good behaviors; punishment makes you explore ways to evade the punishment—so it’s terrible for “nuanced behaviors.”

The thread’s peak is the moment it stops being a clever metaphor and becomes an everyday diagnostic tool. AskYatharth turns it into a felt experience: avoidance in high-dimensional life creates “little jitters” (swimming-pool flailing), while approach requires “wading” toward something with your whole body. Then Ocean stress-tests the slogan in public before publishing the blog post; Romeo Stevens cheers because the phrase is finally “short and punchy,” and adds a second grenade: “Punishment is goodhart waiting to happen”—people can fake “good” and miss rewards, but they can also contort themselves to ensure punishment doesn’t happen and call that success. Adele comes back with a physics analogy (sucking vs blowing fluids) to argue the asymmetry is structural, not just vibes.

What fizzles out is the hope that a single clever counterexample kills it. actualhog tries: what if you constrain wicked desires with “hyperplane” punishments—just fence off murder/rape so the remaining attractors win? The replies don’t really dethrone the idea; they shift it into its proper niche: punishment can define boundaries (“electrified fence lines”), but it still doesn’t give you a precise destination. The concept then metastasizes into side-quests—edsaperia says awayness is easier to agree on politically (rights-based societies), relic_radiation applies it to parenting/therapy (“don’t give kids extra problems”), and tr_babb goes full sci-fi: pain is like gradient updates in neural nets, so training AIs might literally be inflicting suffering.

Why care: if you’re trying to change behavior—your own, your kid’s, your team’s, or an RL agent—this thread is a warning label. “Stop doing X” is cheap and socially popular, but it mostly produces evasive optimization and anxious jittering. If you want *steering*, you need an explicit “towards” target (and maybe some fences), not just louder sticks.
